structure.title: 3. Research designs (multi-state firm design; CPS design)
4. Employment in multi-state firms (main, robustness, alternative estimators, reallocation)
5. Salaries and posted wages in multi-state firms

observations.statement: The identifying assumption is stated explicitly in the introduction: conditional on establishment and firm-by-year fixed effects, intra-firm employment across establishments would have evolved similarly absent the reform. The design is named a multi-state firm design and linked to prior work using within-firm comparisons.
observations.quote: conditional on the included establishment and firm-year fixed effects

observations.statement: The introduction names policy endogeneity (reforms driven by larger recession shocks), mean reversion, and competing state reforms as threats, and previews how each is addressed with alternative control groups and exclusions.

The design section presents an event-study regression with establishment and firm-by-year fixed effects and a treated-state indicator interacted with event-time dummies; the reference period is t-1; each coefficient is interpreted as the intra-firm difference in outcome growth. The ATT is the reported summary estimand.

Identification is framed as reform timing being as good as random relative to the control states; parallel pre-trends are described as a partial test and robustness checks are framed as exploring policy endogeneity, mean reversion and other policy changes.
observations.quote: One partial test for this is whether the pre-trends are parallel

observations.statement: The single-state reform (North Carolina) is analysed with a standard event study, while the six moderate reform states with staggered dates are pooled and analysed with heterogeneity-robust staggered DiD estimators; North Carolina is separated because it changed both duration and benefit level.

The choice among staggered estimators is justified by data structure and software feasibility: de Chaisemartin and d'Haultfoeuille for models with establishment-level fixed effects, Borusyak et al. for models without them, with Sun and Abraham reported for robustness; memory and convergence limits of Stata commands are cited as reasons.

A separate CPS design is described for data lacking firm identifiers: state and year fixed effects, predetermined individual controls, control states limited to Southern and Midwestern non-reform states, and a staggered estimator for the pooled reforms.

Three proprietary or confidential microdata sources are named with their unit and period: EEO-1 establishment employment (establishment-year), Glassdoor self-reported salaries (person-year), and Burning Glass job ads (establishment-job-quarter); CPS supplements are used as public complements.

The analysis sample is restricted to multi-state firms with at least one establishment in a treated state and one elsewhere; two states with small or temporary duration cuts are excluded throughout, stated in a footnote.

Data coverage is documented for each source: the share of the private workforce covered by EEO-1 by establishment size (appendix figure), the share of online postings and of ads with posted wages in BGT, and cross-source validation from prior literature.
Every regression table reports N, the number of firms, and (where relevant) the number of states in the sample, so the effective number of clusters is visible per column.

The sample window is defined in event time (a fixed number of years before each state's reform through a common end year) and the allocation of partially treated years to pre or post periods is explained separately for each dataset according to when outcomes are measured.

Outcomes are log establishment employment, log starting salary and log posted wage; new hires in Glassdoor are defined by reporting less than one year of relevant experience, with the caveat that this excludes experienced new hires.

A job in the posting data is defined following prior work as the combination of firm, detailed occupation code (crosswalked over time) and job type; firm names are cleaned with code from earlier papers.

Treatment is an indicator for establishment location in a reform state, with reform dates and the magnitude of each state's cut tabulated in a setting table; the average post-reform reduction is defined over the analysis window.

Main tables list event-time coefficients, the ATT, fixed effects rows marked with X, the mean of the dependent variable for not-yet-treated units, N, firms, states and R2 (R2 only for OLS columns); notes state the clustering level and bootstrap replications for the staggered estimator.

Tables pair the North Carolina reform and the moderate reforms as column blocks and vary the control group or sample restriction across columns, with the baseline repeated for comparison in the estimator table.

Because the staggered DiD commands do not return sample summaries, the number of observations and firms is reported from a corresponding reghdfe run, stated in a footnote naming the Stata commands used.

The Glassdoor specification lists individual-level controls in table notes (gender, education, state, metro, sector, job type) and uses job and firm-by-year fixed effects; CPS tables list predetermined characteristics as a row.

Standard errors are clustered at the firm level for multi-state firm analyses and at the state level for CPS analyses; the text states the level but gives no explicit argument for choosing firm rather than state as the cluster.

For the single treated state, a Fisher exact test is implemented by reassigning treatment to each possible placebo state and comparing t-statistics, following Imbens and Rubin; the authors explain why it is infeasible for the pooled staggered design (combinatorial count and hours per estimation).
A footnote records that the authors considered a design-based cluster variance estimator and rejected it citing a subsequent paper on its applicability to quasi-experiments.
For staggered designs the notes state that standard errors are based on a fixed number of bootstrap replications with firm clustering.

For each outcome a three-panel figure shows residualized raw means for treated versus control with the control line shifted to match the pre-period mean, the event-study coefficients with confidence bars, and the staggered event-study; pre-period coefficients are also reported in tables.
Pre-reform summary statistics by treated and control status are placed in an appendix table, with the text noting that identification relies on parallel trends rather than level balance.
observations.quote: our identification strategy relies on parallel trends, not level balance

observations.statement: Policy endogeneity is probed with a supplementary figure of UI trust fund balances per covered worker for reform versus other insolvent states, normalized in the pre-reform year, and with a footnote comparing UI tax rates before and after.

Compositional selection of new hires is checked by predicting an above-average wage indicator from CPS demographics and using that prediction as the outcome in a staggered DiD; the coefficient is reported only in a footnote.

Establishment counts by event time and an establishment exit regression on an unbalanced panel are reported in footnotes to check that the balanced panel is not affected by differential entry or survival.

Alternative control groups (states with insolvent trust funds; insolvent states with a similar recession shock) are reported as extra columns of the main employment table, with the state lists placed in an appendix table.

Competing policy changes are handled by dropping states with right-to-work changes, minimum wage changes, Medicaid expansion, and major corporate or personal tax reforms, one at a time, in a dedicated table; the text notes when a column loses precision because few control states remain.

A single table varies the fixed-effect saturation (firm+state+year; establishment+year; establishment+firm-by-year) and, for the staggered case, reports three heterogeneity-robust estimators side by side; the text uses the contrast to argue for firm-specific trends.
Results for the unrestricted sample of all firms and for single-state firms are placed in an appendix table and discussed as applying to different populations and to a less saturated design.
observations.locator: Section 4.3; Table A3 and A8 references

observations.statement: The wage analyses repeat the full employment robustness battery (alternative controls, policy exclusions, fixed effects and estimators, all-firm and single-state samples, Fisher test) but relegate the tables to the supplement and summarize them in a paragraph.
observations.locator: Sections 5.1 and 5.2; Tables A5 to A10 references

observations.statement: The confounding tax reform in the single-state case is handled by bounding: literature elasticities are used to compute the share of the employment effect attributable to tax changes, with a delta-method standard error on the lower bound reported in a footnote; a sign argument bounds the wage effect.
For posted wages, a check drops firms with no pre-reform wage variation across establishments (national wage setters) and reports how much the sample shrinks.

Heterogeneity is reported as sample splits motivated by UI relevance: starting salaries above versus below a salary threshold (appendix), and posted wages for high versus low exposure occupations defined from pre-reform CPS unemployment and tenure durations (main text table with panels).

The reallocation-versus-net-growth question is tested by dropping tradable industries and by examining indirectly treated establishments (non-reform-state establishments of firms with reform-state presence) against firms without such presence, restricting to non-national firms to improve comparability.

The sign pattern across outcomes (employment up, wages down) is used as an argument that a labour supply shock rather than labour demand or mean reversion drives results; the discussion maps results to search models and to a two-channel wage model.

Posted wages for the same job are used as an outcome immune to composition and match quality, contrasting with realized starting salaries; the paper motivates this with a thought experiment before presenting results.

An implied labour demand elasticity is computed by dividing the employment ATT by the posted wage ATT with a delta-method standard error, and benchmarked against historical and minimum-wage elasticity estimates in a footnote.

CPS effects are expressed relative to the mean employment rate and mean unemployment duration; the divergence from prior literature is explained by reform size, permanence, timing in a recovery, and the within-firm design versus border county-pair designs.

When a robustness column becomes insignificant the text attributes it to fewer remaining control states or a larger standard error rather than to a change in point estimate; a footnote discusses why standard errors do not shrink with sample size in the unrestricted sample.

Acknowledged limitations include a contemporaneous state tax reform, inability to observe match quality or new-hire composition in salary data, possible uncategorized policy changes, and that the multi-state firm sample may over-represent national wage setters, biasing effects toward zero.

Generalizability is addressed by noting that large establishments covered by EEO-1 employ most workers, and by framing the setting (large permanent cuts during a recovery) as a reason findings differ from other contexts.

Figures combine residualized raw trends and event-study coefficient plots with confidence bars; tables use three-level stars; notes repeat data source, sample period, estimator, mean definition and clustering; appendix tables and figures are numbered with an A prefix and referenced as Supplementary Material.

The setting is documented with a table listing each reform's date, duration rule and benefit change, and a figure plotting combined maximum benefit duration in levels and logs for treated, moderate and control groups.
Many secondary estimates (tradable-only, nontradable, exit, composition, delta-method SEs, establishment counts) are reported as numbers inside footnotes rather than in tables.

The introduction states three contributions, previews the two key findings with the identification logic, and ends with a roadmap; setting and data precede the design section; first-stage style evidence on UI receipt is moved to a supplementary appendix and summarized in a short subsection.

Each outcome section presents the main figure and table first, then a robustness subsection, then alternative specifications, then a mechanism subsection; a discussion section after results interprets magnitudes against theory and literature before the conclusion.
The supplement carries the UI receipt and unemployment analysis, balance statistics, state lists, and all wage robustness tables; the main text keeps only employment robustness tables.
observations.locator: Appendix B and Tables A1 to A10 references

observations.statement: A Zenodo replication package DOI is given; each proprietary source is described with how it was obtained and where new requests go; public data are included in the package; the authors commit to reasonable assistance. Stata commands are named in a footnote.

EEO-1 data were accessed under an intergovernmental personnel agreement, Glassdoor data via a data-sharing arrangement with its chief economist, BGT data by purchase, and CPS extracts from IPUMS and CEPR with access dates in the references.

concordance.paper_says: Event-study OLS with high-dimensional fixed effects for North Carolina; de Chaisemartin and d'Haultfoeuille staggered estimator for moderate reforms with establishment-level FE; Borusyak et al. where no establishment FE; Sun and Abraham for robustness.

gaps: No explicit justification for clustering at the firm rather than the state level in the multi-state firm design.
No explicit test statistic for joint pre-trends is reported in the text beyond visual and coefficient-level evidence, although the code calls a joint placebo test.
No preregistration or ethics statement (not expected for this administrative design).
No discussion of multiple testing across the many outcomes and samples.
Supplementary Appendix B and Tables A1 to A10 are not included in the text file, so appendix practices are recorded only from main-text references.

reading.note: All 33 pages of the published text were read, including references. The online supplementary material (Appendix B, Tables A1 to A10, Figures A1 to A3) is not part of the file and was not read.
